meta.description: Open games at your level, court schedules, tournaments in a dozen formats and a rating recalculated after every match. Padel, tennis, table tennis, badminton, squash, pickleball. iOS, Android, web and Telegram.

hero.eyebrow: Padel · Tennis · Table tennis · Badminton · Squash · Pickleball
hero.title: Finding a fourth takes longer than the game
hero.subtitle: That is padel's real problem. Not technique, not courts — three other people free on the same evening and roughly your level. RabbitMatch does that part. It also keeps your rating, runs your tournaments, and shows which hours are still free at the courts near you.

audiences.title: Four different people, one app
audiences.lead: A player looking for a game. An organizer running a tournament. A coach filling a schedule. A club watching occupancy. Until now that was four group chats, two spreadsheets and one administrator who answers in the evenings.

items.title: Players
items.text: Open games nearby, already filtered to your level. A rating that moves after every match. And a real breakdown of your own game: which side of the court you are stronger on, when you win more often, how you hold up in deciding sets.

items.title: Organizers
items.text: From an Americano to a month-long championship. Draws and standings compute themselves, and anything that goes wrong you fix yourself, mid-event, without waiting on support.

items.title: Coaches
items.text: A profile with prices and specialisations, a schedule students book directly, reviews. The reputation stays yours even if you change clubs.

items.title: Venues
items.text: Your free hours reach people looking for somewhere to play tonight. Plus a CRM and occupancy analytics.

how.title: Five steps and you are on court
how.lead: Not one phone call to an administrator.

items.title: Install the app
items.text: iOS, Android, browser or Telegram. Same account everywhere. Through Telegram it takes about thirty seconds — you do not even invent a password.

items.title: Say what you play and where
items.text: Sport, city, rough level. Guess the level: the rating corrects it over your first few matches.

items.title: Take a spot, or create your own game
items.text: The feed shows who is short of people: format, time, venue, spots left. Creating your own takes a minute and puts it in front of everyone who fits the level.

items.title: Book the court
items.text: The clubs in your city in one list, with the hours still free on the day you picked and what they cost. Pick an hour and go play.

items.title: Play, then enter the score
items.text: Everything else follows: rating, history, leaderboard, statistics.

features.title: The parts nobody else builds
features.lead: Half the padel apps out there are a calendar with a Join button. Past that point is the reason we built this.

items.title: Matching that explains itself
items.text: Level, interests, court side, age. Under each name it says why this person suits you — instead of just "recommended".

items.title: Your game, analysed
items.text: Which side of the court you are stronger on. Which day and hour you win more often. What happens at one set all. Who you actually play well with. We have not seen this in any other racket-sport app.

items.title: Tournaments at any size
items.text: An evening for four, a draw for thirty-two, a championship that runs for a month. Rotations, seeding and the table are the app's problem.

items.title: A rating you can trust
items.text: Recalculated after every match and adjusted for the level of everyone on court. Next to it you can see how many games stand behind the number, so nobody inflates one with a couple of lucky evenings.

items.title: Marks from the people you played with
items.text: Anonymous and specific: not a score out of five but "strong serve, stamina drops off". They build the chart of your strengths.

items.title: The city's courts in one list
items.text: Free hours, prices, a filter by time of day. Plus an alert when an evening opens up at the venue you wanted.

why.title: The comparison, without false modesty
why.lead: Clubs are usually choosing between us, an international booking app, and a spreadsheet.

items.question: What does it cost a player?
items.answer: Playing, finding games, creating them, keeping a rating and entering tournaments is free. There are PRO and MAX subscriptions that open up the deeper analytics and some extras. The court itself you pay for at the venue, and that money is theirs.

items.question: Which sports?
items.answer: Padel, tennis, table tennis, badminton, squash and pickleball. Padel is where most of the play is and the tournament formats were built around it. Rating, player matching and statistics work across all six.

items.question: Do I have to install anything?
items.answer: No. There is a full web version and a Telegram Mini App with the same account and the same data. The native app is only more convenient for notifications.

items.question: I am a beginner. Will I be put in with people who wipe the floor with me?
items.answer: Every game carries a level range and you only see the ones you fit. Beginners are visible to each other. If you have never held a padel racket, read our guide first — it covers the rules and why there are walls.

items.question: Which cities does it work in?
items.answer: Games, tournaments, rating and coaches work anywhere there is somebody to play with. Live court availability is connected in Tbilisi so far, and we add cities as clubs come on board.

items.question: How does a club connect?
items.answer: Through the form at the bottom of this page. Setup takes about two days: courts, schedule, prices, staff training. The first two months are free.

hero.title: Play, don't negotiate
hero.lead: The average padel evening starts three days early and runs to a hundred messages in a group chat. We removed that part.
points: A feed of open games already filtered to your level
Partner matching on level, interests and court side
A rating from every match — and how well confirmed it is
A breakdown of your game you will not find anywhere else

stats.label: to play, create games and run tournaments

match.title: Not "recommended" — here is why
match.lead: A list of people in your city, sorted by how good a game the two of you would have. Everyone gets their own: a high rating on the other side is not an advantage here, closeness to yours is.

items.title: Level first
items.text: You cannot play with someone from another league however many interests you share. So level weighs more than everything else put together.

items.title: Left looks for right
items.text: Two people used to the same half of the court rarely make a pair. The app takes that into account — and tells you which side each person plays.

items.title: Interests off the court
items.text: A hundred-odd tags from football to board games. Padel is the game you go for coffee after, and shared subjects work about as well as a shared level.

items.title: The line under the name
items.text: "87% level match, plays the left side, shared interests: football, business, board games." Without that line any match list reads as a random order.

items.title: And a nudge once a week
items.text: Only when the match is genuinely strong and you have never played together. Nothing good found, nothing sent.

items.title: Likes and messages
items.text: Like someone's profile. If it is mutual you both hear about it, and you take it to direct messages from there.

stats2.title: A breakdown, not one win rate
stats2.lead: All of it visible only to you: this is an analysis of your own play, not a public shop window.

items.title: Court side
items.text: Win rate on the left and on the right. Half of all players have stood on the same side for years without once checking it is the right one.

items.title: When you play better
items.text: Weekday against time of day. For some people it really is Tuesday evening.

items.title: Formats
items.text: Different people win Americanos and group-plus-playoff draws. This shows which one you are.

items.title: Consistency and deciding sets
items.text: How evenly you play, and what happens at one set all. It is immediately obvious whether you fall apart in the closing stages or come alive.

items.title: Partners and opponents
items.text: Who you win with and who you do not. Sometimes it is not the person you invite most often.

items.title: Who you play against
items.text: Your opponents by level. If you have spent years beating weaker players your rating will not move, and here you can see why.

traits.title: Where you are strong, according to the people who played with you
traits.lead: After a game you can anonymously mark what your partners and opponents are good at. Not a score from one to five — actual attributes: consistency, tactics, serve, the lob, playing off the glass. Those marks build a chart in your profile.

items.title: Anonymous
items.text: Otherwise marks like these either never get given, or get given out of politeness.

items.title: Every sport has its own attributes
items.text: Padel has the lob and playing off the glass, tennis has the return and topspin, squash has length control. You mark what that game actually contains.

items.title: Contested parts show up immediately
items.text: If some people called an attribute a strength and others called it a growth area, it lands right in the middle. That is the part of your game worth thinking about.

profile.title: A card worth showing
profile.lead: The profile avatar is not a round photo but a card in the style of sports trading cards: gradient, pattern, a big rating, your place in the city. You pick the colour and the pattern, and some of them unlock through play.

items.title: Your place in the city
items.text: Computed from games, win rate and rating together. Rating alone will not get you into the top.

items.title: Medals and achievements
items.text: Some are awarded automatically from results, some by hand for something particular. Some are permanent, some seasonal.

items.title: Character and profile fields
items.text: Gender, age, city, experience, playing hand, court side. These are also what partner matching is built from, so they are worth filling in.

steps.title: Your first game, step by step

items.title: Sign up
items.text: Telegram, Apple, Google or email. Through Telegram it takes about thirty seconds and you never invent a password.

items.title: Set sport, city and level
items.text: Guess the level. The rating corrects it over your first matches — early on it moves faster, so a newcomer reaches their real place sooner.

items.title: Fill in the profile
items.text: Court side, playing hand, age, interests. Dull, but this is exactly what partner matching is built from.

items.title: Take a spot, or create a game
items.text: The feed shows who is short of players. Creating your own takes a minute and puts it in front of everyone at the right level.

items.title: Play and enter the score
items.text: Rating, history and statistics take care of themselves.

items.question: Is it really free?
items.answer: Playing, finding games, creating them, keeping a rating and entering tournaments — yes. There are PRO and MAX subscriptions that open the deeper analytics and some extras. The court you pay for at the venue.

items.question: I do not have three friends who play.
items.answer: That is the normal case and the app was built for it. Most games in the feed are posted by people short of one or two players. You join theirs, or post yours and let it fill.

items.question: Where does my level come from?
items.answer: It starts from your own guess at sign-up. After that the rating is recalculated after every game, adjusted for the level of everyone on court: beat stronger players and you gain more, lose to weaker ones and you drop further. The first matches move it faster so a newcomer reaches their real level sooner.

items.question: How much can I trust the rating?
items.answer: Next to the number you can see how many games stand behind it and whether it has been confirmed by play. A rating someone set for themselves and has not yet backed up is flagged as such and does not enter the city top list. That way the top of the table is people who actually played, not people who typed a seven at sign-up.

items.question: Who marks my attributes?
items.answer: Only people you actually played with. Anonymously: you will not see who marked you, and your partner will not know you marked them.

items.question: What does it run on?
items.answer: iPhone, Android, any browser, and Telegram as a Mini App. One account, one set of data.

meta.title: For organizers: tournaments in a dozen formats, and audience analytics
meta.description: Americano, Mexicano, divisions, groups and playoffs, court ladders, Swiss, a multi-week championship. Draws and standings compute themselves and mistakes are fixed mid-event. Plus analytics on your audience.

hero.title: Arithmetic is not your job
hero.lead: Pairings, rotations, who has not played whom, the running table, who owes what for the court. It is arithmetic, and arithmetic is exactly where amateur tournaments fall apart. Set the format and stop counting.
points: A dozen formats, from a four-player Americano to a month-long championship
Draws, rotations and seeding generated automatically
The table recomputes as scores come in
Made a mistake or lost a player? You fix it yourself, not through support

control.title: The tournament runs, and life keeps happening
control.lead: Somebody pulls a back in round three. The wrong score gets entered. The event gets marked finished a round early. In most services that is a support ticket and a ruined evening. Here it is three taps and you have fixed it yourself.

items.title: Swap a player mid-tournament
items.text: Who replaces them and for how many rounds is your call. The rounds the departing player already played stay in the record rather than vanishing with them.

items.title: Drop somebody into an empty slot
items.text: Arrived five minutes after the start — not a problem. The free place is filled straight from the roster.

items.title: Correct a score already entered
items.text: Typed the wrong number, fix it. The table recomputes immediately for everyone.

items.title: Roll a result back
items.text: Delete a result and every player's rating returns to what it was before that match, and the standings rebuild. Nothing is left miscounted.

items.title: Undo a start or a finish
items.text: Hit "Finish" too early — put the tournament back in play and carry on. Started with the wrong line-up — undo the start.

items.title: All of it without a support ticket
items.text: The organizer owns the tournament. Nobody waits on a chat reply while twelve people stand on court.

formats.title: Plenty to choose from
formats.lead: Americano and Mexicano turn up in every app. What follows is what almost nobody has.

items.title: Americano and Mexicano
items.text: In Americano the partner changes every round on a fixed schedule, so everyone plays with everyone. In Mexicano the next round is drawn from the current table, which keeps games level all evening. Both come in individual and team versions.

items.title: Divisions
items.text: A ladder of championships. The first division is the strongest; at the end of a cycle the best move up and the worst move down. It fits a club that plays with the same crowd every week.

items.title: Groups + playoffs
items.text: The classic. Groups are seeded in a snake by rating so they come out even in strength, then it is knockout.

items.title: Court ladders
items.text: Courts stacked top to bottom, the first one called the Throne. Winners climb, losers drop, and a win on a higher court is worth more. There are versions in fixed pairs and a version where one player leaves the court rather than a pair — there everyone answers for themselves.

items.title: Swiss system
items.text: Each round the opponents are picked to make the match as even as possible while keeping your partners across the event as varied as possible. On equal points whoever drew the stronger opponents ranks higher.

items.title: A championship over several weeks
items.text: A group of four to six pairs, everyone plays everyone, then playoffs. Times are not scheduled: opponents agree between themselves and set the match. The stages have deadlines, and it runs itself from there.

items.title: Draws and rotations
items.text: Built from the format and the entry list. Change the number of courts mid-event and the schedule rebuilds around it.

items.title: A live table
items.text: Scores go in from any phone and the table updates for everyone at once. There is nothing left to argue about.

items.title: A reserve list of its own
items.text: People who did not get a spot wait in the reserve. Somebody drops out, you move a reserve player into the roster with one tap.

items.title: Entry fee as a real field
items.text: An amount and a currency, not a line in the description. It shows on the card, works in filters, and payment details attach to the game.

items.title: Private games
items.text: You decide who gets into the roster and who sees the join code. The game still shows in the feed — hiding it from everyone is rarely what you want.

items.title: Notifications instead of your messages
items.text: Round starts, court assignments, changes, results. Plus game alerts: a player sets their conditions once and hears about every game that fits.

audience.title: Who comes to your games, in numbers
audience.lead: A separate tab in your profile: not "how many events you ran" but who turns up to them and whether they come back. Plus an anonymous rating from participants.

items.title: Repeat attendance
items.text: The organizer's number. Everyone comes once; the second time is only the people who enjoyed it.

items.title: Popular formats
items.text: Which formats actually fill up, and which ones you keep running out of habit.

items.title: Average player level
items.text: What level shows up to you. It tells you whether to announce the next one for beginners or the opposite.

items.title: Gender, age and interests
items.text: A portrait of your audience. It hints at what conditions and what times to pick.

items.title: Activity by time of day
items.text: When people actually go out to play. It usually disagrees with when you schedule games.

items.title: Your core players
items.text: The people who come most often. The whole event rests on them, and theirs is the opinion to ask first.

steps.title: From idea to final in four steps

items.title: Create the tournament
items.text: Format, date, venue, courts, player limit, level range. Two minutes and the draw structure exists. If the format is unfamiliar, there is a "how do you play this" button right next to its name.

items.title: Fill the field
items.text: Send the link to your regulars, or publish it to the feed so players in your city at the right level register themselves. Anyone who does not fit goes to the reserve.

items.title: Run it from your phone
items.text: Start rounds, enter scores, watch the table. Anything that goes wrong is fixed on the spot.

items.title: See how it went
items.text: Final table, every match on record, updated ratings for everyone, and anonymous feedback from the players.

items.question: What does running a tournament cost?
items.answer: Creating and running them is free, with no cap on how many. Some of the heavier formats and the deeper audience analytics can sit behind a subscription.

items.question: What is the difference between Americano and Mexicano?
items.answer: In Americano the rotation is fixed in advance: everyone plays with everyone regardless of results. In Mexicano each round is built from the current table, so people near each other in the standings end up on the same court. Americano is the more social one and suits a mixed group; Mexicano keeps games close to the last round and suits a regular club night.

items.question: How many players fit?
items.answer: From four up to a large draw, depending on the format and how many courts you have. The app checks in advance whether your field fits the schedule given your courts and round length.

items.question: A player left in the middle. What now?
items.answer: Replace them mid-event — you choose who steps in and for how many rounds. The rounds the departing player already played stay in the record. No support ticket needed.

items.question: We entered the wrong score. Can it be fixed?
items.answer: Yes. Scores can be corrected, and a result can be deleted outright — every player's rating then returns to what it was before that match and the standings rebuild. A mistakenly pressed "Finish tournament" is undone the same way.

items.question: Do participants need the app?
items.answer: They need an account, which they can create in a browser or in Telegram without installing anything. Without it there is no live table and no result in their rating.

meta.title: What is padel — rules, court, scoring and how to start
meta.description: A plain guide to padel: how the game works, what the court and walls do, how scoring runs, what equipment you need, and how to play your first game.

hero.title: What padel is, and why it took over
hero.lead: Padel is a doubles racket sport played on an enclosed court roughly a third the size of a tennis court, where the walls are part of the game. It is the fastest-growing racket sport in the world, and the reason is simple: a complete beginner can play a real rally in their first hour.
points: Always doubles — four players, two per side
Enclosed court, 20 × 10 metres, glass and mesh walls in play
Solid stringless racket, underarm serve
Tennis scoring: 15, 30, 40, game, set

basics.title: Six things that make padel padel

items.title: It is always doubles
items.text: Four players, two a side. Singles padel exists on a narrower court but is rare. This is the single biggest reason padel is social: you never play it alone, and you rarely play it with the same three people twice.

items.title: The court is enclosed and small
items.text: 20 metres by 10, surrounded by glass and metal mesh, with a net across the middle. About a third of a tennis court, which means far less running and far more time near your partner.

items.title: The walls are in play
items.text: After the ball bounces on your side, it may come off the back or side wall and you can still return it. This is what keeps rallies alive and why points last much longer than in tennis.

items.title: The serve is underarm
items.text: You bounce the ball and hit it below waist height, diagonally into the opposite service box. There is no serving power advantage, which removes the barrier that keeps beginners out of tennis.

items.title: The racket is solid
items.text: No strings — a perforated composite blade, shorter than a tennis racket. Less power, more control, and much more forgiving on mishits.

items.title: Scoring is borrowed from tennis
items.text: 15, 30, 40, game; six games with a two-game margin takes the set; best of three sets takes the match. If you know tennis scoring, you already know padel scoring.

start.title: How to play your first game

items.title: Do not buy anything yet
items.text: Almost every club rents rackets, and balls are usually included in the court fee. Wear trainers with a decent grip and sports clothes. Buy a racket after five or six games, when you know whether you actually like it.

items.title: Find a beginner game, not a beginner court
items.text: Padel is only fun when the four players are roughly matched. Look for games explicitly marked for beginners rather than booking a court and hoping. In RabbitMatch these are filtered by level by default.

items.title: Learn three rules and ignore the rest
items.text: Serve underarm and diagonally. The ball must bounce on your side before it hits a wall. You lose the point if the ball hits the wall on your opponents' side before bouncing on the floor. Everything else you will pick up from the game.

items.title: Play from the back at first
items.text: Beginners tend to hug the net and get lobbed. Start further back, let the ball come off the wall, and hit it after it drops. The wall is your friend before it is your problem.

items.title: Book the next one before you leave
items.text: The single biggest predictor of whether someone keeps playing padel is whether the second game is already in the calendar. Take a spot in the feed while you are still on court.

vs.title: How it differs from the game everyone compares it to
vs.lead: Both use a net, a court and tennis scoring. Almost everything else is different, and the differences all point the same way — padel is easier to start and harder to dominate.

items.title: Court size
items.text: Padel: 20 × 10 m, enclosed. Tennis: 23.77 × 10.97 m for doubles, open. Less ground to cover, shorter distances, far kinder on knees.

items.title: Racket
items.text: Padel uses a solid perforated blade with no strings and no handle length to speak of. Tennis uses a strung frame. The padel racket generates less power and demands less technique to make clean contact.

items.title: Serve
items.text: Underarm and below the waist in padel — nobody serves aces past you. In tennis the serve is often the whole point. This is the difference that makes a padel beginner competitive on day one.

items.title: Walls
items.text: Padel balls stay in play off the glass. Tennis balls are out. Rallies in padel run far longer, which is more exercise and more fun for the same hour of court time.

items.title: Format
items.text: Padel is doubles by default; tennis is commonly singles. Four people per booking splits the court cost and makes the sport inherently social.

items.title: Learning curve
items.text: Most people can hold a rally in padel within an hour. Tennis usually takes weeks of lessons before a rally is possible at all. Padel's ceiling is still very high — the entry is just much lower.

items.question: What is padel, in one sentence?
items.answer: Padel is a doubles racket sport played on a 20 × 10 metre enclosed court where the glass and mesh walls are part of play, using a solid stringless racket, an underarm serve and tennis scoring.

items.question: Is padel the same as pickleball or paddle tennis?
items.answer: No. Pickleball is played on a badminton-sized court with a perforated plastic ball and no walls. Paddle tennis is a different American game. Padel is the enclosed-court, glass-walled sport that originated in Mexico in 1969 and spread through Spain and Argentina.

items.question: Do I need to be fit or have played tennis before?
items.answer: Neither. The court is small, the serve is underarm and the racket is forgiving, so beginners can rally in their first session. Tennis experience helps slightly with timing and hurts slightly with technique — padel rewards placement over power.

items.question: How many people do I need?
items.answer: Four. That is the main practical barrier to playing padel, and it is why apps that match players by level exist — most games are formed from people who did not previously know each other.

items.question: What equipment do I need to start?
items.answer: Trainers with grip and sports clothing. Rackets are rented at nearly every club and balls are usually included in the court fee. Wait until you have played several times before buying a racket.

items.question: How long does a game last?
items.answer: Courts are typically booked in 60 or 90 minute slots. A full best-of-three-sets match takes roughly 90 minutes; a social session usually plays as many games as fit the booking.

items.question: How is padel scored?
items.answer: Exactly like tennis: points run 15, 30, 40, game. Six games with a margin of two wins a set, and a tie-break is played at 6-6. Matches are best of three sets.

items.question: Can the ball hit the wall on the serve?
items.answer: The serve must bounce in the diagonal service box first. After that it may touch the side or back wall and remain in play — but if it hits the metal mesh before bouncing on the floor, the serve is a fault.

cookies.title: Cookie Policy
cookies.body:
Operator: Individual Entrepreneur Dmitrii Tunguskov
Email: info@rabbitmatch.pro
Effective date: 01.01.2026
Last updated: 28.05.2026
URL: https://www.rabbitmatch.pro/legal/cookies

1. What Are Cookies

1.1. Cookies are small text files stored on a User's device when they visit the web version of the Application. In mobile apps and the Telegram Mini App, similar functionality is provided by local storage (localStorage), session storage (sessionStorage), and other tracking technologies.

2. Types of Cookies We Use

| Type               | Purpose                               | Retention              | Consent Required |
| ------------------ | ------------------------------------- | ---------------------- | ---------------- |
| Strictly Necessary | Authentication, security, session     | Session / up to 1 year | No               |
| Functional         | Language, UI preferences              | Up to 1 year           | No               |
| Analytical         | Usage analysis, error tracking        | Up to 2 years          | Yes              |
| Marketing          | Personalized advertising, retargeting | Up to 1 year           | Yes              |

2.1. Strictly Necessary Cookies are used for:
• User authentication and session security;
• Remembering booking progress;
• CSRF token protection.

2.2. Analytical Cookies. We use the following analytics tools: Google Analytics, Amplitude, Mixpanel.

2.3. Marketing Cookies are only used with explicit User consent.

3. Third-Party Cookies

3.1. The Application may use cookies from:
• Telegram — for authentication and Mini App functionality. Policy: https://telegram.org/privacy
• Google (Google Auth, Google Analytics, if applicable)
• Infrastructure services (Railway, Expo) — technical cookies

4. Managing Cookies

4.1. Users may at any time:
• change Cookie preferences in the Application's Cookie Settings Center (if available);
• opt out of analytical and marketing cookies via the Cookie banner;
• clear cookies in the browser settings;
• use browser extensions to block cookies.

4.2. Disabling strictly necessary cookies may prevent use of the Application.

4.3. In Telegram Mini App, localStorage management is handled through Telegram client settings.

5. Legal Basis

5.1. Cookies are processed on the following legal grounds:
• Strictly necessary cookies — legitimate interest of the Operator;
• Analytical and marketing cookies — User consent (GDPR Art. 6(1)(a)).

Last updated: 28.05.2026

1. Subject Matter

1.1. These Rules govern the booking of sports venues through the RabbitMatch Application.

1.2. The Application acts as an intermediary platform between Users and venue owners. The Operator is not the owner or lessor of courts and is not liable for the physical condition, surface quality, availability of equipment, or other characteristics dependent on the venue owner.

2. Booking Process

2.1. The User selects a venue, date, time, and duration.

2.2. The system checks the availability of the selected slot.

2.3. The User confirms the booking and pays via the Application's payment service.

2.4. After successful payment, the User receives a booking confirmation with a unique order number.

2.5. The booking is confirmed only upon successful payment.

3. Rights and Obligations

3.1. The User must:
• arrive at the court at the booked time;
• comply with venue rules;
• not transfer the booking to third parties without approval;
• notify the Operator of cancellation in accordance with the Refund Policy.

3.2. The Operator may:
• cancel bookings for technical reasons with a full refund;
• suspend booking access for Users who repeatedly violate rules or cancel bookings 2 times per month;
• change booking prices with 12 hours' notice.

3.3. The Operator is not liable for:
• force majeure (weather, venue closure, health restrictions);
• court quality and condition;
• venue owner actions after confirmation;
• injuries or health damage on the premises.

4. Special Conditions

4.1. Uncoordinated advertising at the venue. It is prohibited to use the reserved court for commercial events or promotions without prior approval from the Operator.

4.2. Booking on behalf of an organization. If a User books a court for an event with a commercial component (paid tournaments, sponsored events), the User is obliged to notify the Operator and obtain written consent.
